newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-Murdoch's Super League set for 1997 kick-off.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-Murdoch's Super League set for 1997 kick-off.

text.p: Media baron Rupert Murdoch is set to launch his controversial Super League in Australia in 1997 after a court on Friday ruled that attempts to stop the rebel rugby competition violated anti-monopoly laws.

The Federal Court of Australia upheld Murdoch's appeal against an earlier court ruling in favour of the sport's national body, which banned his breakaway rugby league from kicking off in Australia before the year 2000.
The ruling leaves Murdoch open to launch his league next year. Super League was originally scheduled to start in March 1996.
The Chairman of the Australian Rugby League (ARL), the sport's national organisation, said the court ruling meant there would now be two rugby leagues in the country.
"The situation now is that it looks as though there is going to be two competitions," Ken Arthurson told reporters, without saying when he thought Super League might begin.
He said the ARL would consult its lawyers about a possible appeal to a higher court.

Phil Gould, the ARL-loyal coach of the state side New South Wales and Sydney City club, said two competitions would damage the sport, which has already seen 1996 attendances drop as a result of the battle for control of rugby league.
"No doubt rugby league is in a bit of chaos. Certainly two competitions is going to be damaging to the game," Gould told reporters.

Murdoch has invested A$270 million (US$213 million) in Super League, winning the loyalty of eight existing Australian clubs and more than 200 players. He has also signed up clubs in Britain and New Zealand with the official backing of their national ruling bodies.

Murdoch has been embroiled in a bitter power struggle with the ARL for almost two years. His News Ltd media organisation, a subsidiary of global media giant, News Corp Ltd, has provided the financial backing for Super League.
Murdoch was forced to shelve plans for a Super League kick-off at the start of the 1996 season in March, after losing an earlier court battle with the ARL in February.
The earlier court ruled that the clubs must honour loyalty agreements binding them to play in the existing ARL premiership competition until the end of the 1999 season.
But the federal court on Friday said it found the loyalty clauses linking clubs with the ARL contravened sections of Australia's anti-monopoly trade practices act.

"Since the commitments and loyalty agreements are void, the full court has decided that the trial judge's orders, in so far as they were based on the assumption that the agreements are enforceable, cannot stand," the court said in its ruling.
"The result of the present appeal...is that the appeals have been allowed and all orders made by the trial judge have been set aside," the court said.
However, the court ruled that Murdoch's News Ltd must pay damages to the ARL for the disruption caused during the 1995 season as it had encouraged clubs to breach their contracts with the ARL.
But it limited damages to the 1995 season, saying it was the only year covered by valid contracts between clubs and the ARL.

This seriously limits the damages payment as the 1995 season experienced bumper crowds, unlike the 1996 season which was delayed from starting because of the legal battles over the game and subsequently experienced poor crowds.
